nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

questions.q: A new team member asks how Git differs from GitHub. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the two?
choices: Git is a distributed version control system that runs locally; GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform built on top of Git repositories
Git and GitHub are two competing implementations of the same protocol; teams pick one or the other based on whether they prefer a CLI or a web UI
GitHub is the original software and Git is a lightweight client that was later open-sourced by GitHub for users without web access to the platform
Git is the centralized server component and GitHub is the desktop client that synchronizes a working copy with the central Git repository over HTTPS
questions.explanation: Git is an open-source, distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005. It runs entirely locally — every clone of a Git repository contains the full history. GitHub is a commercial platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features (pull requests, issues, Actions, Projects, etc.) on top of Git. Git works without GitHub; GitHub requires Git. The two are not competing implementations of the same protocol — GitHub builds on Git, not alongside it. GitHub did not invent Git; Git predates GitHub by three years and was open-sourced by Torvalds. And Git is not a centralized client/server system — there is no single authoritative Git server that everyone synchronizes against.

questions.q: A developer edits a file and runs `git commit -m "fix bug"`, but the commit completes with no changes recorded. Which step did they most likely skip?
choices: Running `git pull` first to refresh the remote tracking branch so that the new commit does not conflict with any upstream changes from collaborators
Running `git add <file>` to stage the modified file, since `git commit` only records changes that have been added to the staging area beforehand
Running `git init` again to ensure the working directory is registered as a Git repository before any new commits can be recorded on the branch
Running `git push` immediately before the commit so that the change is uploaded to the remote and then included in the new commit on the branch
questions.explanation: Git uses a three-area model: working directory, staging area (index), and repository. `git commit` only records what has been explicitly staged with `git add`. A modified file that has not been staged is invisible to `git commit`, which is why the commit completed but recorded nothing. `git pull` synchronizes with the remote and is never required to make a local commit. `git init` is run once per repository — re-running it does not affect staging and is not what is missing here. `git push` uploads existing commits to the remote and therefore cannot logically precede the commit it is supposed to publish.

questions.q: A team wants log files generated under `logs/` to never be tracked by Git, regardless of which developer creates them on their local machine. What is the standard approach?
choices: Add a `.gitignore` file at the repository root containing `logs/`, then commit the file so every clone of the repository inherits the same ignore rules
Configure a global `~/.gitignore` rule on each developer's machine so that the `logs/` directory is skipped by Git on every individual system independently
Run `git rm -rf logs/` after every commit so that any log files inadvertently staged are removed before they reach the remote main branch automatically
Set the `logs/` directory to read-only at the filesystem level so that Git's commit step cannot capture changes to files inside that directory at all
questions.explanation: A committed `.gitignore` at the repository root applies to every clone — every developer automatically inherits the same ignore rules. Patterns like `logs/` exclude that directory from being staged or committed. A global `~/.gitignore` is for editor backup files and OS metadata that vary per machine; it cannot enforce a team-wide rule because each developer would have to configure it. `git rm -rf` after every commit is reactive and error-prone, and does not stop files from being staged in the first place. Filesystem read-only bits do not stop Git from tracking files that are already committed, would break local logging, and are easy for any developer to revert.

questions.q: An external contributor without write access wants to propose changes to an open-source repository. Which workflow is the standard GitHub model for this situation?
choices: Open an issue describing the desired change and wait for a maintainer with write access to implement and commit the requested code on the contributor's behalf later on
Request collaborator access on the original repository first, then create a feature branch in that repository and open a pull request against the `main` branch from there
Clone the repository locally, create a patch file with `git format-patch`, and email the patch to the maintainers for them to apply manually to the main branch of the project
Fork the upstream repository into the contributor's own account, push commits to a branch in the fork, and open a pull request from the fork back to the upstream repository
questions.explanation: GitHub's standard contribution model for users without write access is fork-and-pull-request. The contributor forks the upstream repository into their own account, pushes commits to a branch in their fork, then opens a pull request from `their-fork:branch` to `upstream:main`. Opening an issue surfaces a request but does not propose any code, leaving the contributor unable to demonstrate the fix. Asking a maintainer to grant collaborator access before contributing is uncommon for first-time contributions to popular open-source projects and is granted at the maintainer's discretion. Emailed `git format-patch` patches are the pre-GitHub workflow and are not the platform's native flow — PRs supersede them.

questions.q: A reviewer opens the Files changed tab of a pull request to leave feedback on specific lines. Which statement about line comments on a pull request is accurate?
choices: Line comments are private notes visible only to the reviewer who wrote them and the pull request author; other reviewers cannot see them anywhere in the PR
Line comments can be posted individually as single comments or batched into a single review with an overall verdict of Approve, Request changes, or Comment
Line comments require the reviewer to have admin rights on the repository because they trigger a status check that blocks merge until each comment is cleared
Line comments automatically resolve and disappear when the pull request author pushes any new commit to the branch, even if the commented line is unchanged
questions.explanation: On the Files changed tab a reviewer can either add a single line comment that posts immediately, or start a review and accumulate multiple comments that are submitted together with a verdict of Approve, Request changes, or Comment. Line comments are visible to everyone with access to the pull request, not private to the reviewer and author. New commits do not auto-resolve threads — they remain until someone explicitly marks them resolved, which preserves the discussion history. Reviewers need read access only; line comments do not require admin rights, and they do not by themselves create a merge-blocking status check.

questions.q: A maintainer wants contributors who open new bug reports to fill in specific fields like reproduction steps and environment details in a structured way. Which GitHub feature is designed for this?
choices: A pinned issue at the top of the issues tab containing a markdown template that contributors are expected to copy by hand into a new issue when filing a bug
A repository wiki page named "Bug Report" that defines the required fields, which contributors are asked to read and follow before they open any new issue
An issue form or issue template stored under `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` that pre-populates the body of a new issue with structured fields when New issue is clicked
A required GitHub Actions workflow on `issues: opened` that closes any new issue whose body does not match a regular expression covering the mandatory fields
questions.explanation: GitHub issue templates and the newer issue forms live in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`. When a contributor clicks New issue, GitHub presents the available templates and pre-populates the body with the chosen one — or renders structured form fields with their own validation. Pinned issues just keep one issue visible; contributors must still manually copy any content into a new issue, so they enforce no structure. Wiki pages document the desired format but are equally voluntary and not surfaced in the New issue flow. A workflow that auto-closes issues missing certain fields is technically possible but punitive, and it is not GitHub's native mechanism for collecting structured bug reports.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: A maintainer wants new contributors to be able to start working on the project in a preconfigured cloud development environment with one click, without installing any tools locally. Which GitHub feature provides this?
choices: GitHub Pages, which serves a static documentation site from the repository at a free `github.io` address with optional custom domain configuration available
GitHub Codespaces, which provisions a containerized cloud development environment defined by a devcontainer configuration committed inside the repository
GitHub Packages, which hosts container images of the development environment that contributors then pull and run on their own local Docker installation first
GitHub Releases, which attaches a versioned VM image to each tagged release that contributors download and boot in their local hypervisor of choice manually
questions.explanation: GitHub Codespaces provisions a cloud-hosted development environment running in a container, with the toolchain, dependencies, and editor (VS Code in the browser or local) pre-installed based on a `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` file in the repository. Contributors click Code → Codespaces and are coding within seconds with no local installation. GitHub Pages publishes static documentation sites — it has no terminal, compiler, or runtime. GitHub Packages distributes container images and other artifacts but still requires the contributor to run them on their own machine. GitHub Releases bundles build artifacts to a tag; it does not provide a runnable cloud environment.

questions.q: A team tracks work across multiple repositories and wants a single board with custom fields (Status, Priority, Iteration) that can pull in issues and pull requests from any of those repositories. Which GitHub feature fits this need?
choices: A repository-level Project (classic) board, which is scoped to a single repository and shows To do, In progress, and Done columns with a fixed card model
A milestone, which groups a set of issues from one repository under a shared due date and shows progress as the linked items get closed or reopened over time
A pinned issue in each repository listing the work items as a markdown checklist, kept in sync by a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow that runs once every night
A GitHub Projects board at the user or organization level, which supports custom fields and pulls in items from any repository the user has access to in one view
questions.explanation: The newer GitHub Projects (sometimes called Projects v2) can be created at the user or organization level and supports custom fields (single select, number, iteration, date, etc.), multiple views (table, board, roadmap), and items drawn from any repository the project has access to. Classic Projects are scoped to a single repository (or one organization-level board) with a fixed column/card model and no custom fields. Milestones are repository-scoped and only show due-date progress against linked issues. Pinned issues with checklists synced by Actions are a brittle workaround, not a real project-management surface, and have no field schema.

questions.q: A repository depends on third-party libraries declared in `package.json`. The owner wants pull requests automatically opened whenever a dependency has a known vulnerability with a fix available upstream. Which feature delivers this?
choices: Code scanning with CodeQL, which performs static analysis of the source code on every push and opens issues for any vulnerable function calls it detects in code
Secret scanning, which inspects commits for accidentally committed credentials and opens pull requests to rotate any matching tokens with their respective providers
Dependabot security updates, which monitors the dependency manifest against the GitHub Advisory Database and opens pull requests that bump to a patched version
Branch protection rules requiring a passing dependency-audit status check, which blocks merges until each contributor manually upgrades the affected library locally
questions.explanation: Dependabot security updates watch manifests like `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, and `go.mod` against the GitHub Advisory Database. When a dependency has a known vulnerability with a fixed version available, Dependabot opens a pull request bumping the version, complete with release notes and compatibility scores. Code scanning analyzes the application source code itself, not the dependency manifest, and does not open version-bump PRs. Secret scanning targets leaked credentials in commits, not vulnerable libraries. Branch protection rules can require a status check to merge, but they do not generate the upgrade pull request themselves — somebody or something still has to make the change.

questions.q: An organization owner wants to require that every member of the organization use two-factor authentication to access organization-owned repositories. Which approach implements this policy natively?
choices: Send an email to each member asking them to voluntarily enable two-factor authentication on their account before the end of the current calendar quarter at the latest
Enable the organization-level setting requiring two-factor authentication for all members and outside collaborators, which removes any account that does not comply
Add a branch protection rule to each repository that rejects pushes from any committer whose linked email is not associated with an account that has 2FA enabled on it
Configure SAML single sign-on for the organization, which inherently enforces 2FA on all sign-ins because every supported identity provider requires 2FA by default
questions.explanation: GitHub organizations have a setting under Security that requires two-factor authentication for everyone in the organization. When enabled, GitHub removes from the organization any member or outside collaborator whose account does not currently have 2FA on, and prevents non-2FA accounts from joining. A voluntary email request is not enforcement — non-compliant accounts retain access. Branch protection rules cannot inspect a committer's 2FA status; they gate code, not authentication factors. SAML SSO controls authentication routing but does not by itself enforce 2FA — that depends on whether the identity provider requires it, which varies by IdP and policy.

questions.q: A developer has finished a feature on a branch and wants their work merged into `main` while giving teammates a chance to review and discuss the changes first. What is the standard GitHub mechanism for this?
choices: Push the branch directly to `main` and then open an issue asking teammates to review the commits that were already merged into the default branch of the repository
Create a release tag on the feature branch so GitHub automatically merges it into `main` once the required number of reviewers have starred the repository for the team
Email a `git diff` of the feature branch to the team and merge locally with `git merge` once everyone has replied with their approval to the email thread out of band
Open a pull request from the feature branch into `main`, which lets teammates review, comment, and approve the changes before they are merged into the default branch
questions.explanation: A pull request is GitHub's core collaboration mechanism: it proposes merging one branch into another and opens a space for review, line comments, approvals, and required status checks before the merge happens. Pushing straight to `main` skips review entirely and inverts the order — the change is already merged before anyone has a chance to comment. Release tags mark versions; they do not trigger merges, and stars are a popularity signal unrelated to review counts. Emailing a diff and merging locally is the pre-GitHub workflow and bypasses every piece of the platform's review tooling.

questions.q: A maintainer wants to publish project documentation as a website served directly from a branch or `/docs` folder of the repository, for free, without standing up a separate web host. Which GitHub feature provides this?
choices: GitHub Pages, which builds and serves a static website from a branch or `/docs` folder of the repository at a `github.io` (or custom) domain
GitHub Gists, which host shareable code snippets and render them as a multi-page documentation website with navigation when marked public
GitHub Wikis, which automatically deploy the repository's `README.md` as a public, indexed marketing site at a dedicated `pages.github.com` address
GitHub Packages, which serves rendered HTML documentation to anonymous visitors after the docs are published as a versioned package artifact
questions.explanation: GitHub Pages publishes a static site straight from a repository — you pick a branch (often `main` or `gh-pages`) and optionally a `/docs` folder, and GitHub serves it at `<user>.github.io/<repo>` or a custom domain, free for public repos. Gists host individual snippets, not multi-page sites, and their public toggle has nothing to do with site generation. Wikis provide per-repository documentation pages browsable inside GitHub but are not the static-site publishing surface and do not deploy the README to a public domain. Packages distributes build artifacts (npm, Maven, container images, etc.) — it is a registry, not a web host.

nodes.title: Microsoft 365 licensing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Microsoft 365 is sold in subscription plans that bundle productivity apps, security, and device management. MS-900 exams test which plan includes which features and the volume licensing options.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Business vs Enterprise plans — key split?
flashcards.back: Business plans (Basic/Standard/Premium) are capped at 300 users. Enterprise plans (E1/E3/E5) have no user cap and include advanced compliance and security features.

flashcards.front: What does Microsoft 365 E5 add over E3?
flashcards.back: E5 adds advanced security (Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps), advanced compliance (Purview), and Power BI Pro — roughly doubles the cost of E3.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Volume Licensing vs Microsoft 365 subscription?
flashcards.back: Volume Licensing (EA, CSP) offers negotiated pricing, centralised management, and payment flexibility for large organisations; subscriptions are per-user/month via direct or partner channels.
Office 365 is the older brand for productivity apps + cloud services. Microsoft 365 adds Windows 10/11 Enterprise licences and advanced security/compliance tools.

questions.q: A founder pushes their company's source code to a brand-new public repository on GitHub without adding any license file. A passerby asks whether they are now free to reuse the code in their own product. What does the absence of a license mean?
choices: Public visibility automatically places the code in the public domain, so anyone may copy, modify, and redistribute it for any purpose without restriction
GitHub applies the permissive MIT License by default to every public repository that does not include its own explicit `LICENSE` file at creation
Without a license the default copyright applies, so others may view and fork it on GitHub but have no granted rights to use, modify, or distribute the code
An unlicensed public repository may be used freely for non-commercial purposes only, while any commercial reuse requires written permission from the author
questions.explanation: Under copyright law, code is owned by its author the moment it is written; without a license, no usage rights are granted to others. On GitHub, the Terms of Service still let people view and fork a public repo (those are forum-style functions of the platform), but reuse, modification, and redistribution are not permitted absent an explicit open-source license. Public visibility does not place code in the public domain — that requires an explicit waiver such as CC0. GitHub does not auto-apply MIT or any other default license; the project author must choose one. And copyright law does not bake in a non-commercial-use exception — that only exists when a license explicitly says so.

questions.q: A first-time user of GitHub Copilot in their editor asks what it actually does while they type. Which description is most accurate?
choices: It is a required cloud compiler that builds and runs the project on GitHub's servers, returning the program output inline so no local toolchain is needed
It is a static analysis security scanner that reviews each saved file for vulnerabilities and refuses to let the file save until every finding is resolved
It is a hosted CI service that runs the test suite on every keystroke and displays passing or failing status directly in the editor's gutter as code is typed
It is an AI pair-programmer that suggests lines or whole functions of code in the editor based on the file's context, which the developer can accept or ignore
questions.explanation: GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant that offers autocomplete-style suggestions — from a single line to a whole function — based on the surrounding code and comments; the developer accepts, edits, or ignores them. Copilot does not compile or execute code on GitHub's servers; building and running stays local or in CI. It is not a security scanner that blocks file saves — that role belongs to code scanning / CodeQL, which runs at push or PR time, not on save. And it is not a CI test runner — running the suite on every keystroke is the job of GitHub Actions and per-project test runners, not Copilot.

questions.q: An organization owner wants to grant the five-person `frontend` team write access to a set of repositories without assigning permissions to each developer one by one. What is the recommended GitHub approach?
choices: Create a team in the organization, add the five members to it, and grant that team the desired repository access so all members inherit it
Add each developer as an outside collaborator on every repository individually, since organization teams cannot be granted repository-level permissions
Share a single shared machine-user account among the five developers and grant that one account write access to each of the relevant repositories
Make all five developers organization owners, which is the only role that confers write access to the organization's repositories at scale
questions.explanation: Teams are GitHub's mechanism for managing access at scale: you create a team, add members, and grant the team a permission level (read/triage/write/maintain/admin) on repositories, and every member inherits it. Changing the team's access once applies to all members and to any future additions automatically. Adding each person as an outside collaborator defeats the team model and is intended for non-members. A shared machine-user account violates security best practice (no individual attribution, no per-user 2FA enforcement, no revocation when someone leaves). Making everyone an owner grossly over-grants privileges, since owners control billing and the entire organization, not just write access to selected repos.

questions.q: A contributor writes a commit message `Closes #42` and merges the pull request containing that commit into the default branch. What happens to issue #42?
choices: Issue #42 is permanently deleted from the repository along with all of its comments, because closing keywords remove the referenced issue entirely
Nothing changes automatically; closing keywords work only inside the issue's own comment thread and have no effect when written in a commit message
Issue #42 is automatically closed and linked to the pull request when keywords such as `Closes`, `Fixes`, or `Resolves` merge into the default branch
Issue #42 is converted into a pull request so the two items merge into a single thread, since linking keywords combine an issue and a PR into one record
questions.explanation: GitHub recognizes closing keywords — `Close`/`Closes`/`Closed`, `Fix`/`Fixes`/`Fixed`, `Resolve`/`Resolves`/`Resolved` — in commit messages and pull request descriptions; when the change merges into the repository's default branch, the referenced issue is automatically closed and cross-linked to the PR. Closing an issue never deletes it — the issue and its full comment history remain available, which is essential for audit and search. The keywords are recognized in commit messages and PR bodies, not only in issue comment threads. And issues are never converted into pull requests — they are distinct object types that get linked together, not collapsed into one record.
